articles.title: Why developers need room to experiment, learn, and build without turning every idea into a business
articles.description: Imagine spending your weekend building something interesting.  Maybe a small weather application.  A...
articles.body_html:
Imagine spending your weekend building something interesting.

Maybe a small weather application.

A tool that organizes your photographs.

A website that recreates the interface of an old computer.

Or a simple Python script that solves a problem nobody else seems to care about.

You spend hours experimenting.

Something breaks.

You fix it.

You learn something new.

And finally, the project works.

You're happy.

Then someone asks:

"That's interesting. How are you planning to monetize it?"

And suddenly, a perfectly enjoyable weekend project becomes a business discussion.

What's the target market?

What's the revenue model?

How will you acquire users?

Can you scale it?

Is there an investor opportunity?

I understand these questions. I'm a founder myself.

But I've been thinking about something lately.

Why does everything we build need to become something we sell?

We Have Turned Building Into a Business Competition

There was a time when building software was also a way to explore technology.

You learned HTML because you wanted to create a website.

You experimented with Python because you were curious about automation.

You built a game because you enjoyed playing games.

You created a small tool because something bothered you and you wanted to fix it.

Not every project needed customers.

Not every experiment needed a market.

Not every repository needed thousands of stars.

Sometimes, the project existed for one reason.

You wanted to see whether you could build it.

But the conversation around software development has changed.

Today, we frequently hear:

Build in public.

Launch an MVP.

Find paying users.

Create recurring revenue.

Turn your skills into a business.

There's nothing wrong with any of these ideas.

In fact, I believe they're valuable when you're intentionally building a company.

The problem begins when we start applying the same expectations to every experiment.

A Side Project Has a Different Job

A startup exists to create value for customers through a sustainable business.

A side project doesn't necessarily have that responsibility.

It might exist to help you learn.

To explore an unfamiliar technology.

To understand how something works.

To test an unusual idea.

Or simply to enjoy the process of creating something.

Consider someone building a tiny operating system as a learning exercise.

It probably won't compete with Linux or Windows.

Does that mean the project has failed?

Of course not.

The developer might learn more about memory management, process scheduling, and hardware than they would from months of watching tutorials.

Or consider someone building a small application that visualizes sorting algorithms.

There are already hundreds of similar tools.

From a business perspective, the idea might appear unoriginal.

From a learning perspective, it could be incredibly valuable.

A project's value isn't always measured by how many people will pay for it.

Sometimes its value is what it teaches the person building it.

AI Has Made This Pressure Even More Interesting

AI has reduced many of the barriers to creating software.

You can prototype an idea faster.

Generate boilerplate.

Explore unfamiliar frameworks.

Build interfaces.

Experiment with APIs.

That's wonderful.

But there's a strange consequence.

Because building has become easier, the pressure to produce something commercially useful can become even greater.

Why build a small experiment when you could launch an application?

Why learn a framework when you could create a SaaS product?

Why spend time exploring an idea when you could turn it into a business?

I think this misses something important.

Just because technology makes an opportunity possible doesn't mean we have to pursue it.

We should be able to experiment without having to justify every hour through a potential financial return.

Otherwise, curiosity slowly turns into another performance target.

Sometimes the Most Interesting Projects Are Completely Impractical

Think about the projects developers enjoy sharing.

Someone creates a programming language for fun.

Someone builds a robot that performs a ridiculous task.

Someone turns a terminal into a game.

Someone recreates an old interface.

Someone connects a sensor to a Raspberry Pi just to understand how it works.

These projects may not solve enormous business problems.

But they can be fascinating.

They encourage experimentation.

They teach unexpected lessons.

And sometimes they inspire other developers to try something new.

Not everything useful has to begin with a commercial purpose.

In fact, some of the most interesting ideas emerge when people are free to experiment without knowing exactly where the results will lead.

That's one reason I don't want us to lose the culture of building things simply because they seem interesting.

I Believe in Distribution. But Not Everything Needs Distribution.

This is where my perspective as a founder becomes important.

I've written before about how developers can build global influence without working at Big Tech.

I believe in sharing knowledge.

I believe in building relationships.

I believe developers should understand how to reach people with their work.

And when you're building a company, distribution is absolutely essential.

A product that nobody discovers will struggle, regardless of its technical quality.

But here's an important distinction.

A project you build for learning is not the same as a product you're building for customers.

The first doesn't need a marketing strategy.

The second probably does.

The first can succeed even if only one person uses it.

The second needs a sustainable reason to exist in the market.

Both are legitimate.

The mistake is pretending they're the same thing.

The Hidden Cost of Monetizing Every Idea

Turning an experiment into a business changes your responsibilities.

Suppose you build a small application over the weekend.

You enjoy the process.

You share it with a few friends.

Everything is simple.

Now imagine deciding to commercialize it.

Suddenly, you may need:

  • customer support and documentation
  • billing and payment systems
  • security and privacy considerations
  • reliable hosting and monitoring
  • maintenance and updates
  • marketing and customer acquisition
  • financial and operational planning

None of these responsibilities are inherently bad.

They're part of building a real product.

But they can fundamentally change your relationship with the project.

Something that previously gave you creative freedom can become another obligation.

And sometimes, the financial opportunity isn't large enough to justify everything that comes with it.

A side project can be successful precisely because it remains a side project.

We Shouldn't Confuse Learning With Wasted Time

Imagine a developer spending two weeks creating a small game.

They don't sell it.

They don't launch a startup.

They don't gain a large audience.

But they learn about state management, event handling, rendering, and application architecture.

Was that time wasted?

I don't think so.

The project might make them a better developer.

It might introduce them to a new field.

It might help them discover something they genuinely enjoy.

And that learning could become valuable years later in a completely different context.

Not every return on effort is immediate.

Not every useful skill can be assigned a price.

Sometimes the most valuable outcome is that you understand something today that you didn't understand yesterday.

There's Nothing Wrong With Wanting to Build a Business

I don't want this article to sound anti-startup.

Quite the opposite.

Building a business is one of the most challenging and rewarding things someone can attempt.

I know that entrepreneurship requires discipline, patience, judgment, and an enormous amount of work that happens outside the technical product.

If your intention is to create a business, you should think about customers, distribution, pricing, competition, and financial sustainability.

You should validate demand.

You should understand the market.

You should ask whether the problem is valuable enough for someone to pay to solve it.

But you don't need to apply that process to every interesting idea.

I wrote in I Think Developers Are Building Too Much Software about the importance of knowing what deserves to be built.

There's another side to that argument.

Sometimes something deserves to be built even when it has no commercial value.

Because the purpose might be learning, creativity, or enjoyment.

And those are perfectly valid reasons.

Maybe We Need Two Different Definitions of Success

For commercial products, success might mean:

Are customers using it?

Does it solve a valuable problem?

Will people pay for it?

Can the business sustain itself?

For personal projects, the questions can be different.

Did I learn something?

Did I solve an interesting challenge?

Did I enjoy building it?

Would I like to explore this technology further?

Did it make me a better thinker or developer?

We need both kinds of work in the technology community.

Commercial projects create economic opportunities.

Personal experiments create space for curiosity and discovery.

And occasionally, something built purely out of curiosity becomes a useful product.

That's wonderful when it happens.

But it doesn't need to be the expectation.

My Advice to Developers: Keep Something Just for Yourself

If you're a developer, I would encourage you to have at least one project that doesn't need to prove anything to anyone.

No business model.

No growth target.

No investor pitch.

No pressure to make it viral.

Build something because you find it fascinating.

Experiment with a language you've never used.

Recreate something from your childhood.

Build a useless little tool that makes you smile.

Explore a difficult algorithm.

Try combining two technologies that don't normally belong together.

You might discover something useful.

You might build something terrible.

You might abandon the project halfway through.

That's fine.

Not every experiment needs to become a success story.

Sometimes the freedom to fail without financial consequences is exactly what makes experimentation worthwhile.

The Best Part of Building Might Be the Building Itself

I spend a lot of time thinking about technology, business, and the future of AI.

I believe technology should solve meaningful problems.

I believe founders should think seriously about distribution and customer value.

And I believe developers should recognize the opportunities their skills create.

But I also believe we need to preserve something simple.

The joy of creating things.

Not because someone will pay us.

Not because it will improve our personal brand.

Not because an algorithm will reward us.

But because solving a problem, understanding a system, or making an idea come alive can be satisfying in its own right.

We don't have to turn every interest into income.

We don't have to turn every experiment into a product.

And we certainly don't have to turn every side project into a startup.

Sometimes you can build something, learn something, smile at what you've created, and move on.

That's not a missed business opportunity. That's a perfectly good reason to build.

articles.title: JavaScript: The Language That Gaslights Its Developers
articles.description: After writing about PHP's greatest hits in the Weird Language Hall of Fame, it felt only fair to turn...
articles.body_html:
After writing about PHP's greatest hits in the Weird Language Hall of Fame, it felt only fair to turn to JavaScript.

Because if PHP is the language of historical baggage, JavaScript is the language of "this seems impossible, and yet it is fully specified behavior."

JavaScript has a special talent for producing results that look like bugs, feel like bugs, and absolutely are not bugs.

Most of the time, the culprit is type coercion, implicit conversion, or one of the language's many "technically reasonable, emotionally devastating" rules.

So here are a few of my favorite examples.

1. An Empty Array Is Truthy... But Also Equal to false

Let's begin with a classic.

Boolean([])       // true
[] == false       // true
[] === false      // false

This is the kind of thing that makes developers stare at the screen and wonder why they picked computing science instead of accounting like their mom advised.

An empty array is truthy.

So far, so normal:

if ([]) {
  console.log("Yep, truthy");
}

That runs.

But then this also happens:

[] == false   // true

Why?

Because JavaScript doesn't use the same rules for boolean contexts and loose equality.

In a boolean context, arrays are simply objects, and objects are truthy.

But with ==, JavaScript starts converting values. The empty array becomes an empty string, which then becomes the number 0. Meanwhile, false also becomes 0.

So JavaScript ends up comparing:

0 == 0

Which is, unfortunately, true.

And if you really want to ruin your afternoon:

[] == ![]   // true

Because ![] becomes false, and now you're back in the previous example.

The lesson: truthiness and loose equality are not the same thing. If you're comparing values in JavaScript, === should be your default.

2. typeof null Is "object"

This one has survived for decades.

typeof null         // "object"
typeof undefined    // "undefined"
typeof []           // "object"
typeof NaN          // "number"

Let's focus on the weirdest part:

typeof null   // "object"

Except null is not an object.

This is a long-standing historical bug in JavaScript that became untouchable because too much code depended on it.

So now it just lives there, like haunted wallpaper.

And since JavaScript enjoys layering confusion on top of confusion:

  • null is not an object, but typeof null says it is.
  • Arrays are objects, so typeof [] is also "object".
  • NaN means "Not a Number," but typeof NaN is "number".

You can almost hear the language whispering, "If you can't handle me on my worst days, you don't deserve me."

The lesson: typeof is useful, but not always precise. If you need to distinguish arrays, nulls, and objects, use more specific checks like Array.isArray() and explicit value === null.

3. map(parseInt) Produces Nonsense

This is one of the best examples in the entire language because every piece of it looks reasonable.

["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt)

What would you expect?

[10, 10, 10]

What do you actually get?

[10, NaN, 2]

Naturally.

Here's what's happening.

map() doesn't just pass each array element to the callback. It passes three arguments:

  1. the current value
  2. the current index
  3. the whole array

So this:

["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt)

effectively becomes:

parseInt("10", 0)  // 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // 2

And why is that a problem?

Because parseInt() takes a second argument: the radix.

So JavaScript interprets the array index as the number base.

  • "10" in base 0 becomes 10
  • "10" in base 1 is invalid, so NaN
  • "10" in base 2 becomes 2

This is one of those perfect JavaScript moments where two completely legitimate APIs collide and create chaos.

The fix is simple:

["10", "10", "10"].map(Number)

or:

["10", "10", "10"].map(x => parseInt(x, 10))

The lesson: Don't hand a function to map() unless you know exactly what arguments it expects.

4. sort() Sorts Numbers Like Strings

This one has caused real bugs in real applications.

[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort()

What you probably expect:

[1, 2, 3, 10, 20]

What JavaScript gives you:

[1, 10, 2, 20, 3]

Because by default, sort() compares elements as strings.

So JavaScript is effectively sorting these:

  • "1"
  • "2"
  • "10"
  • "20"
  • "3"

And in string comparison, "10" comes before "2".

This makes perfect sense if you're sorting words.

It makes much less sense if you're sorting numbers in a programming language and expected numeric order to be the default.

The fix:

[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort((a, b) => a - b)

Now you get what you wanted:

[1, 2, 3, 10, 20]

The lesson: JavaScript's default behaviors are often optimized for generality, not for your expectations.

So, Is JavaScript Bad?

Not really.

Like PHP, JavaScript is often mocked for behavior that is actually consistent with its own rules.

The problem is that many of those rules are invisible until you trip over them.

An empty array can be truthy while also loosely equal to false.

typeof null can lie to your face.

A perfectly innocent-looking map(parseInt) can produce results that seem like a prank.

And sort() can rearrange numbers alphabetically, because apparently that was a reasonable default choice at some point in human history.

But that's also what makes JavaScript fascinating.

Its weirdness isn't random. It's the product of a language that was created to validate forms in web pages and became something people use to build microservices and large-scale data streaming pipelines, and evolved while the entire internet was standing on top of it.

Which is kind of impressive.

This is part of a series on programming languages that occasionally make developers question the nature of reality.

PHP already had its turn. Python, C#, and Perl are waiting patiently in the wings.

And Perl, as always, remains less a programming language than a dare.

articles.title: Deno 2.9's task cache turns a 4-second build into a 10-millisecond skip
articles.description: I measured Deno's new deno task caching: 3.9s cold against 9ms warm on a real build step, but a 3000-file input tree made the cache check itself about 4x slower than running an untracked task.
articles.body_html:
A deno.json task with a files list now remembers whether it needs to run at all. I hadn't seen this mentioned anywhere, so I built a small, deliberately expensive build step, ran it with and without the new caching fields, and tried to break it.

The short version: a task that took 3.9 to 4.3 seconds dropped to under 10 milliseconds once nothing in its declared inputs had changed. That part works as advertised. What doesn't work the way I expected is the cost of checking in the first place, and what happens when a task writes to a file it also lists as an input.

What the feature actually is

Deno's task runner (deno task, driven by the tasks block in deno.json) now accepts three extra fields on a task definition:

{
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "command": "deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts",
      "files": ["src/**/*.txt", "build.ts"],
      "output": ["dist/**"]
    }
  }
}
  • files is the input glob. Declaring it is what turns caching on at all; a task with no files field always runs.
  • output is the glob of files the task produces. On a cache hit, these get restored from the cache store rather than regenerated.
  • env (not shown above) lists environment variable names whose values also feed the fingerprint.

I ran this against Deno 2.9.8, installed from the official Linux x86_64 build, with no --unstable flag anywhere. This is shipped, stable behaviour, not a preview.

The headline number

My build.ts reads every file under src/, hashes each one 2000 times with SHA-256 to simulate real CPU-bound work, and writes a combined manifest to dist/. Forty source files, about 1.1MB total.

Run Cold (cache cleared first) Warm (cache hit)
1 4.289s 0.0100s
2 4.025s 0.0093s
3 3.939s 0.0100s

Fastest cold run against fastest warm run: 3.939s versus 0.0093s, a 423x difference. All three warm runs printed the same line:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts (cached, inputs unchanged)

No process spawn for deno run, no re-read of the source files, no re-hashing. The task is simply not executed.

It really is content, not timestamps

The cache manifest, which lives under ~/.cache/deno/task_cache_v1/<hash>/manifest.json, records a size and an mtime for every tracked file alongside a content_hash and a static_hash. Seeing mtime sitting right there in the JSON, I assumed it was part of what decided a cache hit, the way plenty of build tools work.

I ran touch src/file_5.txt with no edit to the file's contents, then ran the task again:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts (cached, inputs unchanged)

Still cached. Then I actually appended a line to the same file and ran it again:

Task build deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts
build.ts actually ran

That re-ran, and the following run went back to cached. So the documentation's claim ("the contents of the matching files") holds up under a direct test: mtime and size are a cheap pre-check to decide whether a file is worth reading, not the thing that decides the final verdict. A bare timestamp bump doesn't invalidate anything.

Output really does get restored, not just skipped

The other claim worth checking: that deleting your output directory and re-running a cached task regenerates it. I deleted dist/ entirely, ran the cached task again, and dist/main.txt came back with the exact content the last real build produced, while build.log (a side effect outside the declared output glob, used only to prove whether the command itself re-ran) stayed untouched. The command did not execute. The files were pulled back from the cache store. Both halves of the claim check out.

Where it quietly never helps you

I wrote a task whose files glob included a file that the command itself appends to:

{
  "tasks": {
    "selfmutate": {
      "command": "echo appended >> src/input.txt && echo ran",
      "files": ["src/*.txt"]
    }
  }
}

Run it three times and src/input.txt ends with three "appended" lines. Every run changes the very input it's fingerprinted against, so every run invalidates its own next run. Nothing in the tool warns you about this. If your build step writes a log, a timestamp, or a generated file into the same directory it reads from, caching silently does nothing for you, and you'd have no way to tell short of watching the task actually execute every time.

Two things that used to be bugs and aren't anymore

Deno's own commit history shows a real defect here: for a while, deno task build foo and deno task build bar produced the same fingerprint, because the hash only covered the command string, not the arguments appended after it. I tested this directly on 2.9.8 with a task that just echoes its arguments:

$ deno task argtask -- foo    # first run: executes
$ deno task argtask -- foo    # second run: cached
$ deno task argtask -- bar    # different arg: executes again, correctly

Different arguments get different fingerprints now. Same story for env: a task with "env": ["MODE"] ran fresh under MODE=dev, cached on the repeat, then ran fresh again the moment I switched to MODE=prod, then cached again on the repeat of that. Both the documented behaviour and a previously real bug check out against the current release.

What it costs when the task itself is cheap

This is the finding that argues against the headline number. I built a 3000-file, 12MB input tree and attached it to a task that does nothing but echo noop:

with files tracking (cache hit) no files field at all
Run 1 0.0320s 0.0101s
Run 2 0.0314s 0.0080s
Run 3 0.0346s 0.0106s

Checking whether 3000 files changed cost roughly 3 to 4 times longer than just running the command with no tracking at all, even on a hit. For my 4-second hashing job this overhead is noise. For a task that's already fast, say a lint pass over a small package that finishes in 20ms, attaching files over a large tree could plausibly cost more than it saves. Deno checks file size and modification time before reading contents, which keeps the common case cheap, but on a big enough tree that pre-check alone adds up.

No concurrency protection, and no partial reset

I started the same cold build task from two processes at once, with the cache cleared beforehand:

A: ELAPSED 3.9316s  (actually ran)
B: ELAPSED 4.0020s  (actually ran)

Both ran the full 4-second task in parallel. Nothing serialised them, and nothing let the second one wait for the first and reuse its result. If two CI steps or two editor saves trigger the same expensive task at once, you pay for it twice, not once.

There's also no way to invalidate a single task's cache entry. deno task has no --no-cache flag. The only lever is deno clean, which removes the entire DENO_DIR, not just task_cache_v1:

$ deno clean
Removed /root/.cache/deno (24 files, 607.61KB)

That also wipes the module cache, the npm cache, and everything else Deno stores, which on a real project is a much bigger rebuild than just re-running one build step.

What I got wrong on the way

My first assumption, reading the cache manifest before running a single test, was that the stored mtime field was load-bearing: that touching a file would be enough to force a rebuild, because that's how make and a lot of task runners behave. It isn't. The manifest stores mtime as a cheap filter to decide whether to bother reading a file at all; the actual cache decision rests on the content hash underneath it. I only caught this because I tested the boring case (touch, no edit) before the interesting one (real edit), rather than assuming they'd behave the same.

Run it yourself

This needs only the Deno binary, no Docker and no account:

curl -fsSL https://deno.land/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.deno/bin:$PATH"
deno --version   # I used 2.9.8

mkdir deno-cache-test && cd deno-cache-test
mkdir src
for i in $(seq 1 40); do head -c 20000 </dev/urandom | base64 > "src/file_$i.txt"; done

cat > build.ts <<'EOF'
const files = [];
for (const entry of Deno.readDirSync("src")) if (entry.isFile) files.push(`src/${entry.name}`);
files.sort();
let combined = "";
for (const f of files) {
  let digest = await Deno.readFile(f);
  for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) {
    digest = new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", digest));
  }
  combined += `${f} ${Array.from(digest).map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2,"0")).join("")}\n`;
}
await Deno.mkdir("dist", { recursive: true });
await Deno.writeTextFile("dist/manifest.txt", combined);
console.error("build.ts actually ran");
EOF

cat > deno.json <<'EOF'
{
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "command": "deno run --allow-read --allow-write build.ts",
      "files": ["src/**/*.txt", "build.ts"],
      "output": ["dist/**"]
    }
  }
}
EOF

time deno task build   # cold: several seconds
time deno task build   # warm: single-digit milliseconds

If you want to see the self-mutation pitfall, add a task whose command appends to a file matched by its own files glob, and watch it execute on every run regardless.

What to do with this

Point files only at what the specific task actually reads, never at src/** for a whole repo when the task touches one package, and check first that the command doesn't also write into that same glob, or caching will quietly do nothing for it. And before adding this to something that already runs in under 50ms, time it cold and warm the way I did above. On my 3000-file tree, the fingerprint check alone cost more than that.

articles.title: Cookie-Dependent Content and SEO: Test the Page Without Yesterday's State
articles.description: To diagnose cookie-dependent content for SEO, inspect a public page as a fresh visitor and compare it...
articles.body_html:
To diagnose cookie-dependent content for SEO, inspect a public page as a fresh visitor and compare it with the returning visit your team normally sees. Check the initial response and rendered content separately. If the important answer appears only after remembered state is restored, the familiar browser view may be hiding a discovery problem.

Google documents a specific reason to make this check: its Web Rendering Service does not retain state across page loads, and storage and cookies are cleared across loads. That is documented Google behavior, not a claim about every AI engine. The workflow below investigates the page without bypassing consent, authentication or access controls.

Choose one public answer to trace

Use a concrete content target. Imagine a fictional scheduling product whose public integrations page should explain whether its calendar connection supports two-way updates. Returning visitors see the explanation. A fresh browser shows a short introduction and an empty space where the integration details should be.

The target is that public explanation, not every visual element on the page. Record its expected wording, the URL, the relevant preference state and how a person reaches it. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing buyer answer from a decorative component that merely loads later.

Keep the scope public. A customer's private calendar, account settings and paid application workspace are not material you should expose for SEO. If the answer belongs behind authentication, investigate the public documentation that describes the capability rather than trying to make the private workspace crawlable.

Separate the response from the rendered page

The initial HTML response and the browser's rendered document answer different questions. The response shows what the server sent for the request. The rendered document shows what exists after the browser has executed the page's permitted scripts and processed the resulting changes.

In the fictional example, the response might contain the integration heading but no capability explanation. The returning browser might later populate that explanation from an application component. That observation narrows the investigation; it does not prove a search engine failed to render it.

Use the browser's normal developer inspection tools to examine both views. Note whether the text is absent, present but hidden, or replaced after a preference is loaded. Avoid diagnosing the whole site from a screenshot. A screenshot establishes what was visible in that state, while the response and document help explain how the page reached it.

Compare fresh and returning visits deliberately

Open the public page in a clean browsing session using the site's normal access flow. Record what happens before any optional preference is chosen, then record the result of an appropriate normal choice. Separately inspect the returning session that originally looked correct.

Do not silently change the experiment halfway through. If language, region, consent or sign-in state differs, write that down. A fresh visitor in one locale and a returning visitor in another are not a controlled comparison of cookies alone.

The useful question is whether a prior visit is required for the public answer to exist. If the answer appears after an ordinary action, document that action. If it needs a preference stored during an earlier page load, identify that dependency. At this stage, describe the behavior you can reproduce rather than naming a cause you have not established.

Use Google's rendering evidence for the Google question

Google's JavaScript troubleshooting documentation describes its stateless rendering behavior. It also points to URL Inspection and the Rich Results Test for examining rendered output and related rendering problems. Use the available owner tools and permissions for the site you are auditing.

Compare the relevant text in that rendered evidence with the fresh and returning browser observations. Save the test date and tested URL. A difference deserves investigation; it does not by itself tell you whether cookies, blocked resources, timing or another condition caused it.

Keep this evidence tied to Google Search. A Google rendering test is not a measurement of what ChatGPT, Claude or another answer surface retrieved. It can reveal a public-page problem worth fixing, but engine-specific claims need engine-specific evidence. This boundary prevents a useful technical diagnosis from turning into an unsupported universal AI crawler rule.

Trace the dependency before choosing the repair

Ask the responsible developer where the public text comes from and what conditions allow it to render. In the fictional integration page, perhaps the application waits for a remembered display preference before mounting a component that contains both optional features and essential documentation.

If that dependency is confirmed, the design question becomes smaller: can the public explanation be delivered through the normal public page without requiring yesterday's state? The solution might involve separating essential documentation from an optional interactive component. The appropriate implementation depends on the actual system; this article does not prescribe a framework-specific patch.

Do not solve the problem by serving secret extra claims only to bots. Do not remove required consent protections, expose private data or make a paid feature public to create a successful test. The goal is consistent access to information the business already intends to publish.

Repair the user journey as well as the content dependency

A page can contain the right text and still leave a first-time visitor unable to use it. Check the visible route to the explanation. Does the heading describe the integration question? Does the page state the current support conditions? Can a person reach the relevant documentation without remembering a previous selection?

For the fictional calendar connection, a useful public answer might identify which direction of updates is supported and link to current setup limitations. Those product facts must be verified before publication. Adding a generic paragraph about integration benefits would not repair the missing capability answer.

Keep preference-specific variations understandable. If the site offers localized instructions, explain how a fresh visitor selects the applicable version. Avoid treating every variation as a bug. The issue is an unintended dependency that makes a public answer unavailable or misleading, not the mere existence of a preference.

Retest the same states after the change

Repeat the initial response check, the clean visit and the returning visit against the same content target. Also repeat the relevant Google inspection when available. Capture the text that matters, the URL, date, browser conditions and any actions required to reveal it.

A useful acceptance statement is specific: the public integration explanation is present for a fresh visitor under the intended conditions, and the returning experience still works. This is stronger than saying “SEO fixed,” because it names the behavior actually verified.

Google's technical requirements also make clear that meeting requirements does not guarantee indexing. A successful rendering repair is therefore not proof of an indexing gain, a ranking gain or an AI citation. Track those outcomes separately if they matter to the project.

Leave a diagnosis the next person can repeat

Write a short investigation note with the public question, expected text, tested states, observed differences, confirmed dependency and completed repair. Include what remains unknown. A small record with evidence is more useful than a ticket that says the page looked different in incognito mode.

If the problem cannot be reproduced, retain the original conditions rather than forcing a conclusion. A browser extension, an old session or another environmental difference may need further checking. Report an unresolved discrepancy as unresolved.

For search and AI visibility work, the practical payoff is a more dependable public source. Buyers and search systems still have to discover, interpret and choose that source. Testing without remembered state addresses one concrete failure mode: a team mistaking its familiar returning-user view for the page that a first-time visitor can actually read.

articles.title: Your calculator returns nothing to crawlers. Here's how I fixed it with Playwright.
articles.description: Client-side calculator pages ship an empty div in their HTML source. bingbot doesn't run JavaScript, so it indexes a blank page. A build-time Playwright prerender fixes it — and there are three traps you'll hit.
articles.body_html:
The problem

If your site is "user types numbers → JavaScript computes a result", your HTML source probably looks like this:

<div id="result"></div>
<script src="calc.js"></script>

Users see nothing wrong. Crawlers download 30KB of HTML containing no answer at all.

Googlebot does execute JavaScript, but only when it decides the page is worth rendering — and the render queue can lag days to weeks. bingbot and most other crawlers do not execute JavaScript at all. They get the blank div, index it, and your page competes for "concrete volume calculator" with zero matching text.

I hit this building jianzhujisuan.com — 168 construction calculators, 380 static pages, every result computed in the browser.

The fix: don't solve it at runtime, solve it at build time

One extra build step: open each page in a real browser with default inputs, wait for the JS to finish, capture #result's innerHTML, write it back into the same container in the HTML file.

const { chromium } = require('playwright');

async function prerender(file) {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('file://' + file);        // local file, no server needed
  await page.waitForSelector('#result');

  // Note the (expr)() — see trap 1
  const inner = await page.evaluate(`(${config.capture})()`);

  injectIntoContainer(file, inner);         // into the container, see trap 2
}

Output:

<div id="result">
  <!-- prerender:start fp=a3f8c91b2e4d7a60 -->
  <table><tr><td>Concrete volume</td><td>3.24 m³</td></tr></table>
  <!-- prerender:end -->
</div>

For visitors: calc.js loads and overwrites #result's innerHTML — the static copy disappears, nothing changes for them.
For crawlers: no JS execution, but the table is right there in the source.

Single acceptance test — open the page with javaScriptEnabled: false:

const ctx = await browser.newContext({ javaScriptEnabled: false });
const page = await ctx.newPage();
await page.goto(url);
console.log(await page.textContent('#result'));  // must contain real numbers

Trap 1: page.evaluate("() => x") evaluates, doesn't call

I used a "formula fingerprint" to decide whether a page needs re-rendering — hash the compute function's source, compare against a stored fingerprint, skip if unchanged.

// WRONG
const fp = await page.evaluate('() => window.CALC.fp');

The fingerprint came back empty every time. When page.evaluate receives a string, it evaluates the expression and returns the resulting function object — it never calls it.

function callExpr(expr) {
  return `(${expr})()`;     // becomes (() => x)()
}
const fp = await page.evaluate(callExpr('() => window.CALC.fp'));

The same trap exists in waitForFunction, and it's worse there: a string that evaluates truthy means you waited for nothing and captured a half-rendered result.

Trap 2: injecting before </body> shows users two copies

My first version inserted the block before </body>. Locally, with JS enabled, users saw two result tables — the static one sat outside #result, so the live innerHTML overwrite never removed it.

You have to splice into the container's interior, matching tag depth:

function spliceInner(html, id, inner) {
  const open = new RegExp(`<div[^>]*id=["']${id}["'][^>]*>`);
  const m = open.exec(html);
  if (!m) return null;

  let i = m.index + m[0].length;
  let depth = 1;
  const tagRe = /<div\b|<\/div>/g;
  tagRe.lastIndex = i;

  let t;
  while ((t = tagRe.exec(html))) {
    depth += t[0] === '</div>' ? -1 : 1;
    if (depth === 0) return html.slice(0, i) + inner + html.slice(t.index);
  }
  return null;
}

Now the static block lives inside #result and gets replaced along with everything else.

Trap 3: re-running stacks blocks

A build step must be idempotent. Inserting before </body> gives you three copies after three runs. Wrap the block in markers and replace on re-run:

const BLOCK_RE = /<!--\s*prerender:start[^>]*-->[\s\S]*?<!--\s*prerender:end\s*-->/;
const after = BLOCK_RE.test(before)
  ? before.replace(BLOCK_RE, () => block)
  : inject(before, block);

Second run should report 0 rendered, 1 unchanged. If every run reports "all rendered", your fingerprint is empty — go back to trap 1.

One more thing: lastmod ordering

If your sitemap carries lastmod, the prerender injection must run before lastmod is computed.

Otherwise adding prerender marks all 380 pages as "modified today". Run it again the next day — all 380 pages modified again. From the crawler's perspective your site claims a full-site rewrite every single day, which destroys your sitemap's credibility.

If you must run it daily, strip the injected block from the content fingerprint — the block changed, the page's substance didn't.

Results

380 pages, on a single reused browser instance:

  • Build time: noticeably longer, but it's a one-off cost with a reused single browser instance — never in the user request path
  • Every page returns its full result table with JS disabled
  • Median real body content: 1,655 CJK characters (was ~400 characters of template skeleton)

What prerendering does not fix

It's worth being blunt here. Prerendering fixes "can the crawler see the content". It does not fix "does the search engine want to index you".

I assumed fixing the blank-div problem would fix indexing. It didn't. Two weeks later, bingbot had fetched 2 pages out of 380 and indexed zero. The reason had nothing to do with my HTML — it was a new domain with zero inbound links, and no crawler algorithm allocates crawl budget for a site nobody mentions.

Content visibility and site trust are two separate problems. Prerender solves the first one properly. The second one is a marketing problem, and you solve it by writing things people link to.

Code and verification

The code: calc-prerender — MIT licensed, ~180 lines of Node, a runnable example, and the three traps written up in the README. It is not a demo: this is the script that runs in the production build.

Production case: jianzhujisuan.com — 168 bilingual construction calculators, 380 pages, all built this way. The whole implementation (~180 lines) is what runs in that build pipeline.

Quick verification: open a page like brick count calculator, disable JavaScript, refresh. If the result table is still there, it worked. If you see an empty div, prerendering never ran.

articles.title: Google Translate was crashing our React app — here's how we fixed "removeChild" for good
articles.description: Our most engaged user hit "Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node'" because Chrome was auto-translating the page. Why it happens, how to reproduce it without Google Translate, and the three-layer fix we shipped.
articles.body_html:
I build QRflows, a dynamic QR code platform. Last week I was going through session recordings and found our most engaged user of the month: someone in Hong Kong who spent 11 minutes in the dashboard, clicked 82 times, tried half a dozen QR types, added a logo, built a landing page.

At minute three, the page crashed and reloaded.

The error in the console:

NotFoundError: Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node':
The node to be removed is not a child of this node.

The recording made the cause obvious once I noticed it: the whole dashboard was in Chinese. Our site only exists in English. The user had Chrome's built-in Google Translate turned on.

This is one of those bugs that never shows up in your own testing, because you never translate your own app. Here's what's going on, how to reproduce it without Google Translate, and the three-layer fix we shipped.

Why Google Translate breaks React

React keeps references to the DOM nodes it created, including plain text nodes. When state changes, it updates or removes those exact nodes.

Google Translate doesn't know about React. When it translates a page, it walks the DOM and replaces text nodes with its own <font> elements containing the translated text:

<!-- What React rendered -->
<button>Save</button>

<!-- What the DOM looks like after Google Translate -->
<button><font><font>保存</font></font></button>

The original "Save" text node is gone from the DOM, but React still holds a reference to it. The next time React needs to remove or replace that text, it calls parent.removeChild(textNode) — and the browser throws, because that node is no longer a child of anything.

The same thing happens with insertBefore when React tries to insert something next to a node that Translate has swapped out.

It's a long-standing issue — facebook/react#11538 has been open since 2017 — and it isn't specific to React: anything that holds references to text nodes is vulnerable. If you want the deep dive, Martijn Hols' write-up is excellent.

Which code is vulnerable

The crash needs two things: a bare text node and something conditional next to it. Patterns like these:

// Text sitting next to a conditional element
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  Save
</button>

// Conditional text
{error && error.message}

// Ternary returning strings
<span>{isSaving ? "Saving…" : "Saved"}</span>

// Text mixed with an expression
<p>Uploaded {count} files</p>

Every QR builder has dozens of these: status labels, counters, "Uploading… / Done", plan badges. Which is why the crash hit our most active user and nobody else.

Reproducing it without Google Translate

Waiting for a translated session to show up in your logs is not a test plan. You can simulate what Translate does to the DOM in the browser console:

function fakeTranslate(root = document.body) {
  const walker = document.createTreeWalker(root, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT, {
    acceptNode: (node) =>
      node.nodeValue.trim() &&
      node.parentElement &&
      !node.parentElement.closest('script, style, [translate="no"], font')
        ? NodeFilter.FILTER_ACCEPT
        : NodeFilter.FILTER_REJECT,
  });

  const nodes = [];
  while (walker.nextNode()) nodes.push(walker.currentNode);

  for (const textNode of nodes) {
    const outer = document.createElement('font');
    const inner = document.createElement('font');
    inner.textContent = '译' + textNode.nodeValue; // mark it as "translated"
    outer.appendChild(inner);
    textNode.parentNode.replaceChild(outer, textNode);
  }
  return nodes.length;
}

window.addEventListener('error', (e) => console.log('CRASH:', e.message));
fakeTranslate();

Paste it, run fakeTranslate(), then use the app: switch tabs, toggle options, type into inputs, navigate between routes. Run fakeTranslate() again after each step, because real Translate keeps re-translating new content as it appears.

On our dashboard, switching QR types after this reproduced the exact crash from the recording within a few clicks.

The fix: three layers

There's no single clean fix. What worked for us is three layers, from "never crash" to "fewer weird states".

Layer 1: a DOM guard so the crash can't happen

This is the workaround from the React issue thread: patch removeChild and insertBefore so that, instead of throwing, they skip the operation when the node relationship is no longer what React expects.

// src/lib/domTranslateGuard.ts
export function installDomTranslateGuard(): void {
  if (typeof window === 'undefined' || typeof Node !== 'function') return;

  const proto = Node.prototype as any;
  if (proto.__translateGuardInstalled) return;
  proto.__translateGuardInstalled = true;

  const originalRemoveChild = proto.removeChild;
  proto.removeChild = function (child: Node) {
    if (child.parentNode !== this) {
      console.warn('[dom-guard] removeChild skipped', child, this);
      (window as any).clarity?.('event', 'dom_guard_removeChild');
      return child;
    }
    return originalRemoveChild.call(this, child);
  };

  const originalInsertBefore = proto.insertBefore;
  proto.insertBefore = function (newNode: Node, referenceNode: Node | null) {
    if (referenceNode && referenceNode.parentNode !== this) {
      console.warn('[dom-guard] insertBefore skipped', referenceNode, this);
      (window as any).clarity?.('event', 'dom_guard_insertBefore');
      return newNode;
    }
    return originalInsertBefore.call(this, newNode, referenceNode);
  };
}

Two details that matter:

Install it before React touches the DOM. We call it as the very first thing in the client entry, before hydrateRoot:

// entry-client.tsx
import { installDomTranslateGuard } from './lib/domTranslateGuard';
installDomTranslateGuard();

// ...then hydrateRoot(...)

Keep it out of SSR. It only lives in the client entry, and the typeof window check is a second line of defence. The server never touches Node.prototype.

The trade-off is honest: this hides the error instead of fixing the cause. A skipped insertBefore can occasionally leave a piece of UI missing until the next render. That's why we log it and send a custom event to our session analytics — so we can see how often the guard actually fires, and on which pages.

Layer 2: stop giving Translate bare text nodes

The guard prevents crashes. Wrapping text in elements prevents most of the situations where it would have to step in. If text lives inside its own <span>, Translate replaces the text inside the span, and React only ever adds or removes the span itself — which is still there.

// Before
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  Save
</button>

// After
<button>
  {isSaving && <Spinner />}
  <span>Save</span>
</button>

// Before
{error && error.message}

// After
{error && <span>{error.message}</span>}

// Before
<p>Uploaded {count} files</p>

// After
<p><span>Uploaded {count} files</span></p>

No visual change, no new classes. We went through every component in the QR builder, the file upload flow, the editor and the download modals, and wrapped anything that changes at runtime: status labels, counters, button text next to spinners.

Layer 3: translate="no" — but only where it makes sense

The tempting shortcut is <html translate="no">. Don't. Your users turned on translation because they need it — breaking the crash by breaking the translation just moves the problem.

We only opt out content that shouldn't be translated anyway:

  • URL, email, phone and password inputs
  • short links and destination URLs
  • the QR preview and technical labels (sizes, PNG/SVG)
  • the brand name in the header and footer 
<input type="url" translate="no" />
<span translate="no">{shortUrl}</span>

Everything else — headings, buttons, help text — still gets translated.

How we verified it

After deploying, I ran the fake-translate script on the live site: the public PDF QR generator, then the logged-in dashboard. I switched QR types back and forth, toggled the logo option, typed into inputs, and navigated from the builder to the landing page editor and back — re-running fakeTranslate() after each step.

Result: zero uncaught errors, no reloads, and the UI kept updating live with the "translated" text in place. The brand name and URL fields stayed untouched, as intended.

We'll keep watching the dom_guard_* events in session analytics. If they show up a lot on a specific page, that page still has bare text nodes to wrap.

TL;DR

  • Google Translate replaces text nodes with <font> elements. React still holds the old nodes and crashes on removeChild / insertBefore.
  • You can reproduce it without Translate by wrapping text nodes in <font> from the console.
  • Layer 1: patch removeChild / insertBefore before hydration, client-only, and log when it fires.
  • Layer 2: wrap conditional and dynamic text in <span>.
  • Layer 3: translate="no" only on inputs, URLs and brand names — never on the whole app.

The part that stuck with me: this bug hit the single most engaged user we had that month. International users who translate your app are often exactly the people working hardest to use it.

I'm building QRflows in public — dynamic QR codes with Smart Rules, real-time analytics and a Claude MCP integration. If you've hit this bug with a different framework, I'd like to hear how you handled it.
